Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Sara Lindholm (Elysian CTO), Ravi Kumar (Elysian ML Eng), Lena Ortiz (Elysian Platform)

Summary: quick tech deep dive on prefix caching strategies, focusing on how to maximize hit rate while being safe for multi-tenant workloads, and how caching interacts with batching and quantized models.
Topics: cache keys, hit rate metrics, eviction policies, multi-tenant isolation, VPC/on-prem details, benchmarks.
Action items: see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll run about an hour, Ethan and I will go through prefix caching concepts and then dig into your traces, Sara?
[00:08] Sara: yep sounds good, we have Ravi and Lena on who'll ask the infra and model questions, we also wanted to surface some security constraints up front, like tenant isolation and KMS usage, if that matters for how cache keys are stored or salted.
[00:20] Ethan: great, yeah those are central. quick agenda: 1) cache key design and namespacing 2) hit-rate targets and what to measure 3) evictions/TTL/prefetch 4) multi-tenant safety 5) interactions with batching/KV cache and quantized runtime 6) on-prem/VPC notes and benchmarks.
[00:39] Ravi: perfect. quick context: we serve a chat product with lots of short prompts and some long-form generation. typical prefix reuse is around templates and system messages, but then user messages vary. current infra is GKE with internal redis and a mix of CPU/GPU endpoints, looking to reduce tokens per request and latency.
[01:02] Ethan: ok good, makes sense. first, cache key design. the naive key is just the prefix text, but that's brittle. we recommend canonicalizing, hashing, and namespace by tenant+model+model-variant+prompt-shape. e.g. key = sha256(tenant_id | model_name | model_revision | normalized_prefix). this lets you safely evict per-tenant and avoid collisions.
[01:28] Maya: and important to keep keys deterministic across clients; use a stable normalization (lowercasing, whitespace collapse, remove non-deterministic metadata) and include a version tag in the key so you can invalidate keys after prompt/template changes.
[01:43] Sara: what about PII in prefixes? we need to avoid storing sensitive user content in a cache that might be shared.
[01:49] Ethan: good call — we recommend hashing the prefix before storing and never storing raw text in the cache. Redwood's Managed KV supports envelope encryption and tenant-specific KMS keys in Private deployments; in Hosted we'd use per-customer namespaces plus encryption-at-rest. but still hash the payload so the cache value doesn't contain raw PII.
[02:10] Ravi: got it. does hashing affect hit rates because of whitespace differences or small edits?
[02:16] Ethan: hashing is on the normalized form. small edits will change hash obviously; you can use approximate matching buckets for fuzzier reuse, but that increases complexity and risk of returning stale or mismatched completions. usually we start with exact normalized-prefix hashing, then add heuristics for template variables. for chat apps, extracting system+instruction as one key and user history suffix as separate keys often works.
[02:40] Lena: how do you recommend multi-tenant namespacing? we run many smaller tenants on the same pool.
[02:46] Ethan: namespace by tenant_id as first component, and also scope cache-size / quota per tenant. two patterns: shared cache with per-tenant prefixes and quotas, or create per-tenant logical caches (same backend but distinct key prefixes). shared is more efficient but needs strict quotas and eviction fairness. per-tenant logical caches are simpler for isolation.
[03:08] Sara: and what about cache hits versus model-variant compatibility? like a 8-bit quantized variant might not be interchangeable with full-fp model for all prompts.
[03:16] Ethan: right — key should include model_variant (e.g., model@quant=4bit+ops=true). Redwood's routing will only hit cached prefixes when the serving model is binary-compatible with the cached KV state. we store metadata with each cache entry indicating the model hash and runtime profile. if mismatch, skip cache. this prevents subtle quality regressions.
[03:37] Ravi: can you explain KV cache semantics briefly? I often see confusion between KV cache of transformer past-key-values and our prefix caching layer.
[03:44] Ethan: yeah good distinction. the KV cache inside the runtime is the model's past key/value tensors used for autoregressive decoding. prefix/prompt caching is a higher-level cache that stores either completed hidden-state snapshots or the generated token sequences for a prefix. two approaches: store compiled hidden-state (fast to resume, but very model and quantization sensitive), or store full token outputs for a prefix (more portable but still requires stitching with runtime for continuation). both have tradeoffs for storage size and compatibility.
[04:13] Maya: to add, storing hidden-state snapshots gives huge latency wins because you avoid recomputing early layers, but it couples you to exact model weights, quantization, and even kernel selection. so it's best used in dedicated/private deployments where you control model build. storing token sequences is safer for hosted multi-tenant scenarios.
[04:31] Sara: any numbers on hit-rate expectations? what's realistic for us?
[04:34] Ethan: depends a lot on workload composition. for template-heavy flows we see 60-85% for system+instruction prefixes. for user-generated suffixes it's lower. overall combined hit-rate target is usually 30-50% on early-stage adoption, can get higher with template standardization. important metrics: prefix_hit_rate, prefix_hit_latency (p95), cost_saved_tokens, and false-match rate.
[04:58] Ravi: and how does batching interact? if we batch requests at the runtime, do cached prefixes still help?
[05:04] Ethan: yes; caching reduces per-request compute so batches are lighter. one nuance: if you pre-batch and the cache entry returns a partial KV state, you still need to assemble into the batch. Redwood's runtime supports sticky-batching where cached resumes are co-located to avoid cross-device KV transfer. the biggest win is reducing work per token which improves throughput for shared GPUs.
[05:28] Lena: eviction and TTL — what's recommended? LRU? time-based?
[05:33] Ethan: classic is LRU with size-based thresholds plus TTL. TTL helps when your templates change often. we also suggest soft-eviction signals: bump entry priority based on recency and frequency, and provide a manual invalidate endpoint for operator-triggered template changes. for multi-tenant fairness, use weighted LRU or per-tenant quotas to avoid noisy neighbors.
[05:54] Maya: also include a cache version field so you can invalidate globally when you roll a prompt change. that's safer than trying to expire every key.
[06:02] Sara: what about prefetching — can we precompute likely prefixes during off-peak?
[06:07] Ethan: yes prefetch is powerful. you can run nightly jobs to warm cache for high-traffic tenants or predicted templates. pair prefetch with telemetry to avoid wasted work. prefetching is more cost-effective when storing hidden-state snapshots in dedicated infra because it's cheap to store and huge speed benefits on hit.
[06:25] Ravi: quantization again — is hidden-state snapshot stable across 4-bit quantization? my intuition is it's very brittle.
[06:31] Ethan: correct — hidden-state snapshots are brittle with aggressive quantization. quantization can change distribution of internal activations and kernel paths. if you plan to use hidden-state caching with quantized models, lock the exact quantization configuration and provide the model hash in the cache metadata. we usually recommend snapshot caching only for dedicated or private where you control the runtime.
[06:55] Maya: a practical pattern we've seen: for multi-tenant hosted setups, do token-level prefix caching + per-tenant namespace + strong hashing + TTL/soft-evict. for enterprise/private, you can go for hidden-state snapshots + model-hash binding + stable quantization.
[07:12] Ravi: ok that helps. on the security front, we need to ensure cache can't leak across tenants. you mentioned per-tenant namespaces and encryption — any certifications?
[07:22] Ethan: Redwood's Dedicated and Private offerings support SOC2-level controls, customer-managed KMS, and audit logs. for hosted multi-tenant we enforce logical namespaces and encryption-at-rest; we also support token redaction and hashed keys by default. we'll share the security FAQ doc — we have example policies for RBAC and KMS integration.
[07:40] Lena: network-wise, if we go VPC peering for Private, can the KV cache run inside our VPC so data never leaves the network?
[07:47] Ethan: yes for Private deployments the KV cache and the serving runtime can run inside your VPC or on-prem. Redwood's Private control plane can be configured to not persist raw text outside your environment and to use your KMS. for Dedicated we provide customer-dedicated pools but still managed by Redwood with contractual guarantees.
[08:03] Sara: latency numbers — if we hit cached hidden-state snapshot what's the typical latency improvement?
[08:09] Ethan: depends on model size. for a 7B-ish model we see 2-4x latency reduction on cold-to-resume paths; for LLMs in the 70B+ space, it's often 3-6x because early layers are the most expensive. token-level caching gives less dramatic wins but still reduces token compute and cost. Baseline numbers: uncached p95 generate latency for short prompts ~180-300ms, cached resume paths down to ~40-90ms depending on infra.
[08:36] Raman? sorry whoops — (small filler laugh)
[08:40] Ravi: (laughs) no worries. follow-up: operationally what dashboards should we set up to monitor caching health?
[08:46] Maya: key dashboards: prefix_hit_rate (pct), prefix_miss_latency, cache_evictions/sec, per-tenant cache_size, cache_bandwidth_saved_tokens, false_match_rate, and model_compatibility_mismatches. also track cost savings versus baseline for billing conversation.
[09:05] Sara: any gotchas with A/B testing when caching is on? should we disable caching for fairness?
[09:11] Ethan: a common pitfall — caching can bias A/B test if one variant warms the cache. approach: isolation windows per variant, or tag requests with experiment_id in the cache key and optionally disable cross-variant warm starts. many teams prefer to disable cache for controlled experiments or use per-experiment namespaces.
[09:28] Lena: good point. one more infra question: can cached hidden-state be sharded across GPUs and retrieved efficiently? we run heavy multi-tenant workloads.
[09:36] Ethan: yes, but that requires co-location. Redwood's runtime supports locality-aware placement: cached snapshots are stored on the same node pool and we have fallback policies to fetch from remote if necessary. remote fetch adds latency so locality is critical for performance — that's why dedicated pools help.
[09:55] Maya: want to walk through a quick example with your traces? Ravi, you mentioned you'd share sample prompts; any immediate examples you can paste into chat?
[10:02] Ravi: sure I'll paste three frequent templates... (Ravi pastes examples, audio quirk)
[10:10] Ethan: ok looking at these, the first two are identical system+instruction pairs across sessions — high candidate for prefix-level caching. third one varies user input a lot, so consider token-level caching only on the system part.
[10:25] Maya: recommended implementation roadmap: 1) instrument tracing to emit prefix keys and outcomes 2) run a simulation offline to compute potential hit-rate and cost savings 3) pick caching mode (token-level vs hidden-state) per workload 4) run staged rollout, monitor metrics and false-match rate 5) iterate and expand.
[10:45] Sara: timeline wise we want to pilot within 2-3 weeks if the numbers look good.
[10:49] Maya: that's doable — we'll schedule the staging benchmark and share playbook.
[10:53] Ethan: one more note on cache key salts — if you change normalization rules, include a key-version or salt to avoid accidental collisions. and if you add template variables, prefer placeholder normalization so templates map to same key.
[11:06] Ravi: thanks, that's helpful. any sample configs we can look at for Redis vs in-memory KV vs object store for snapshots?
[11:13] Ethan: yes we'll share a short table in the playbook — tl;dr: Redis/cluster is good for token-level caching with low latency, in-memory on-node is best for hidden-state snapshots in dedicated pools, object store (S3) can be used for large snapshot archives and prefetch pipelines but slower for hot path.
[11:31] Lena: and cost tradeoffs? cheap storage vs expensive GPU cycles?
[11:34] Ethan: exactly — caching trades storage and ops complexity for compute savings. quantify with tokens_saved * cost_per_token (or compute-cycle estimate). Redwood Optimize can help estimate savings given your trace.
[11:46] Maya: ok we'll wrap up with a recap of next steps — share docs, run benchmark, send traces, confirm peering details. any final questions?
[11:54] Sara: none from me, thanks.
[11:56] Ravi: nope, good session.
[11:57] Lena: thanks all.
[12:00] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and scheduling notes.
